response.executive_summary:
This assessment reviewed the Reply Tuner system, which exports closed helpdesk ticket transcripts, uses them to fine-tune a reply model, and surfaces suggested replies to support agents. The review was based on the system-overview documentation and the approved system context.

The assessment resulted in one approved finding, rated high severity. This finding concerns the risk that customer-crafted ticket content can poison the fine-tuning process and the suggested replies generated from the tuned model. If an attacker shapes helpdesk tickets, the resulting training data can encode attacker-controlled behavior into the tuned model artifacts and the suggestions agents see, with potential impact on support quality, policy compliance, and privacy.

Two controls were confirmed: only the Transcript Exporter job identity can write to the Training Store, and suggested replies always require human review before being sent to customers. These controls constrain who can inject training data at the storage layer and ensure that agents remain in the loop for outbound communication, but they do not by themselves address the documented training-data poisoning concern.

No formal documentation gaps were recorded. However, several open questions remain about how requirements for training on untrusted content, governance of tuned model artifacts, data retention, credential management, encryption in transit, and output encoding (req-TRAIN-002, req-TRAIN-003, req-DATA-001, req-DATA-002, req-SECRET-001, req-SECRET-002, req-AI-001, req-AI-004) are defined and implemented for this system. Because these questions are unresolved, the assessment could not determine whether additional relevant controls or weaknesses exist in those areas.
response.system_overview:
The assessed system, Reply Tuner, enhances a helpdesk workflow by fine-tuning a reply model on real customer support interactions and providing suggested responses to agents.

Customers interact with a Helpdesk system by submitting tickets. Support agents work with these tickets through an Agent Console, where they review cases and communicate with customers. Closed-ticket transcripts are the primary training data for the tuning pipeline.

A Transcript Exporter component periodically reads closed-ticket transcripts from the Helpdesk and writes them to a Training Store. The Transcript Exporter operates under a specific job identity, which is the only principal permitted to write to the Training Store. The Training Store holds the training data transcripts asset, representing historical customer–agent interactions used for fine-tuning.

A Tuning Job component reads training data from the Training Store and fine-tunes a Vendor base reply model. The outputs of these tuning runs are Tuned reply model artifacts, which are written to an Artifact Bucket. The Artifact Bucket thus serves as persistent storage for model artifacts associated with particular tuning runs.

The Reply Service loads tuned model artifacts from the Artifact Bucket and uses them to generate Suggested replies in response to ongoing helpdesk conversations. These suggested replies are sent to the Agent Console, where support agents can review, edit, or discard them before sending any response back to customers. Suggested replies are therefore advisory drafts, not automatically delivered messages.

The main actors in this context are Customers, who create helpdesk tickets; Support agents, who use the Agent Console and may act on suggested replies; and the Transcript Exporter job identity, which has privileged write access to the Training Store. The key assets are the Training data transcripts, the Tuned reply model artifacts, the Suggested replies shown to agents, and the Vendor base reply model from which tuned models are derived. No distinct trust boundaries were documented for this architecture; the assessment treated the described components and flows as operating within a single trust domain.
response.risk_summary:
The approved findings indicate a concentrated integrity risk in the training and suggestion pipeline rather than a broad set of unrelated issues. The single high-severity finding focuses on how customer-crafted ticket content can poison the fine-tuning process.

Because closed-ticket transcripts derived from customer submissions feed directly into the Training Store and are then used by the Tuning Job, an attacker who can shape ticket content can influence the Training data transcripts asset. That influence can propagate into the Tuned reply model artifacts and, in turn, into the Suggested replies presented to agents. The impact described includes systematic encouragement of policy violations, disclosure of internal details, or other misleading guidance to agents, potentially degrading support quality and creating privacy or compliance exposure if agents follow harmful suggestions.

The confirmed controls provide partial mitigation but do not eliminate the risk described. Restricting Training Store write access to the Transcript Exporter job identity reduces the chance of arbitrary external modification of stored training data, but it does not prevent poisoning that occurs upstream through malicious yet syntactically valid customer tickets. Requiring that suggested replies always undergo human review before sending ensures that agents have an opportunity to detect problematic suggestions, but it also assumes agents will reliably notice and override subtle or well-crafted manipulations, which the finding treats as an open concern.

No additional weaknesses were approved as findings, and no formal documentation gaps were recorded. Nonetheless, multiple open questions around requirements and controls for training on untrusted content, governance and lineage for tuned model artifacts, data retention and lifecycle in the Training Store, credential storage and rotation for the Transcript Exporter, credential types used with the Helpdesk and cloud platform, encryption in transit for data flows, and encoding or escaping of model outputs in the Agent Console remain unresolved. These questions mean the assessment could not determine whether further risks are present or adequately controlled in those areas; they are not findings but they limit the confidence with which the overall risk posture can be characterized beyond the documented training-data poisoning concern.
